title: The circuit and physical design of the POWER4 microprocessor
decision: Used a relatively simple global clock distribution: a single central PLL driving 64 sector buffers, each driving a tunable sector tree; the 64 trees in turn drive ONE full-chip clock grid at 1024 evenly spaced points. No active or programmable skew-adjustment circuitry was employed.
alternatives_or_rejected: Symmetric buffered H-trees were desired, but silicon and wiring blockages forced more complex tree structures. The paper chose tunable trees driving a single grid over a perfectly symmetric H-tree, and explicitly avoided active/programmable skew-reduction circuitry.
rationale: A single grid driven by tuned trees yields low skew among all ~15,200 clock pins regardless of proximity. The grid is designed very early, creating a stable contract: trees are designed top-down while macro/unit/chip clock wiring proceeds bottom-up in parallel, insulating designers from late grid adjustments. A patented tuning algorithm tuned 2000+ tunable transmission lines; longer wires were split into multiple-fingered transmission lines interspersed with Vdd/Gnd shields for inductance control.
outcome: Achieved 20 ps skew and 35 ps jitter across the 174M-transistor chip at >1.3 GHz; the flatness of the grid (visualized in 3D) confirmed low skew. The method allowed a highly productive combination of top-down and bottom-up design perspectives proceeding in parallel.

title: The circuit and physical design of the POWER4 microprocessor
decision: Set the cycle-time target very early in the project; used detailed simulation of critical timing paths to verify feasibility and structure the pipeline, then aimed to match that performance via custom circuit techniques for most dataflow macros and logic synthesis for most control logic.
alternatives_or_rejected: The paper does not detail alternative partitions, but the chosen approach ('custom design techniques for most of the dataflow macros and logic synthesis for most of the control logic') is described as similar to the prior approach, implying full custom or full synthesis were the alternatives considered/rejected in favor of a mixed approach.
rationale: Early critical-path simulation let the team verify feasibility of the aggressive frequency target and shape pipeline structure before committing. Custom circuits were applied where performance demanded; synthesis was used for control logic to manage the 5-10x complexity increase over prior chips across a multi-site design team.
outcome: Enabled a 174M-transistor chip running at >1.3 GHz; the cycle-time target 'played a fundamental role in defining the pipeline structure and shaping all aspects of the circuit design as implementation proceeded.'

title: The circuit and physical design of the POWER4 microprocessor
decision: Adopted a hierarchical design methodology across four levels, allowing concurrent design across ~1,000 macros by different sites, with the single clock grid acting as an early-frozen contract between top-down tree design and bottom-up macro/unit/chip clock wiring.
alternatives_or_rejected: The paper does not enumerate alternatives, but the chosen 4-level hierarchical, contract-based approach was selected to manage the 5-10x complexity increase over prior chips and a multi-site team; a flatter or less contract-driven methodology would not have supported concurrent development across sites.
rationale: Complexity was 5-10x greater than prior chips, requiring efficient methodology and robust testing to manage power distribution, clocking, and long-wire signal integrity across a multi-site team. The early-frozen clock grid contract insulated macro designers from grid changes while still allowing late-stage grid tuning for skew minimization.
outcome: Allowed the multi-site team to complete the design on schedule; the hierarchical approach with contracted wiring at each level (macro, unit, core, chip) was reported as a key enabler for meeting project goals.

title: The circuit and physical design of the POWER4 microprocessor
decision: Predominantly used static circuits to reduce power-dissipation concerns, while selectively employing dynamic circuits in critical-performance regions; supplemented with low-Vt devices to recover ~10% performance. Embedded ~250 nF of decoupling capacitance; targeted <30 mV average DC drop for power densities up to 1 W/mm^2.
alternatives_or_rejected: Full dynamic-circuit style (higher performance but higher power) vs. full static (lower power but harder to hit frequency) — the paper chose predominantly static with selective dynamic only where needed, balancing power dissipation against the >1.3 GHz frequency target.
rationale: The predominantly-static approach reduced power dissipation concerns while selective dynamic circuits preserved performance in critical regions; low-Vt devices provided a ~10% overall performance improvement. The power network design (with 250 nF decoupling and <30 mV drop target) supported a total chip power of approximately 115 W.
outcome: Achieved >1.3 GHz operation at ~115 W total chip power with <30 mV average DC drop for power densities up to 1 W/mm^2; overall performance improved by ~10% through low-Vt devices.
